title: Track 7, Lesson 3: Three basic ratios to read before buying any share
subtitle: You don't need to be a financial analyst - just enough P/E, ROE and debt ratio to avoid the most basic mistakes.
whyItMatters: These three ratios help you avoid 80% of a new investor's common mistakes: buying a loss-making company without realising, buying one carrying too much debt, or paying far too much for the profits actually being made.
openingQuestion: What does ROE (return on equity) measure?
openingOptions: A ratio reflecting the total sales revenue the company generated over the whole of the past financial year
The gap between the current share price and the overall average index across the entire stock market
The percentage of profit the company decides to return as cash to the shareholders currently holding it
The profit generated on each unit of shareholders' equity
explanation: Three ratios are enough to eliminate most shares not worth buying before you go deeper. P/E tells you how much you are paying for each unit of profit. ROE tells you how efficiently the business uses shareholders' money. Debt to equity tells you what shocks it can survive. All three have to be read together and within one industry: a high ROE alongside very high debt is efficient borrowing, not efficient trading.

diagram.label: Check P/E: what you pay for each unit of profit
Check ROE: how efficiently shareholders' money is used
Check D/E: how much debt is being carried
Compare all three with sector rivals before deciding

realWorldExample.description: Two retailers with the same revenue, but company A has an ROE of 25% while company B manages only 8% - showing that A uses shareholders' money far more efficiently, even though both may report similar revenue.

quiz.question: Is a high debt-to-equity ratio (D/E) always bad?
options: No, the higher the D/E the more effective the leverage
Yes, a D/E above 1 always signals a weak business
Yes, because a high D/E means the business is near bankruptcy
Not absolutely - it depends on the nature of the industry
quiz.explanation: D/E has to be judged in its industry context. Banks run high D/E because that is the business model (taking deposits and lending them on). A manufacturer or technology company with a D/E unusually high for its sector is the signal to be careful about.

quiz.question: You compare two retailers. Company A: P/E 12, ROE 18%, D/E 0.5. Company B: P/E 30, ROE 6%, D/E 2.5. Which looks more attractive on these three ratios?
options: Company A - a lower P/E, a higher ROE, and lower debt too
Company B - the high D/E shows better use of leverage
Company B - a high P/E proves the market expects a lot
There is not enough data to compare these two companies
quiz.explanation: Company A wins on all three: a lower P/E (relatively cheaper), an ROE three times higher (far more efficient), and a D/E five times lower (far safer). When all three ratios agree, the signal is more reliable than reading any one of them alone.

quiz.question: What does an ROE of 20% mean?
options: The company's share price rose 20% over the financial year just ended
The company generates 20 dong of profit for every 100 dong of equity
The company retains 20% of profit and distributes the rest to all shareholders
The company's net profit margin reached 20% measured on total sales revenue
quiz.explanation: ROE measures how efficiently shareholders' money is used. But it can be pushed up by leverage - heavy borrowing shrinks the denominator - so always read it alongside the debt-to-equity ratio.

quiz.question: Why can heavy borrowing make ROE look better than it really is?
options: Because heavy borrowers get tax relief, so net profit rises correspondingly
Because interest paid is added back into net profit when this ratio is calculated
Because heavy borrowing thins the equity, shrinking the ROE denominator
Because high debt forces a company to report higher profits to reassure creditors
quiz.explanation: Two companies with the same profit will show a higher ROE for whichever borrowed more, purely because its equity base is thinner. That is why DuPont analysis splits ROE into margin, asset turnover and leverage.

quiz.question: What are the three minimum questions to answer before buying any share?
options: Foreign ownership, the price band, and the ex-rights trading date
The highest price, lowest price and trading volume over fifty-two weeks
The number of shareholders, the charter capital, and the listing date
Is it profitable, what price am I paying, and is the debt dangerous
quiz.explanation: Skipping the last question is how many people lose everything even when the first two look fine: a profitable company at a fair price can still fail if its debt structure cannot survive one bad year.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't you compare one company's P/E with another's ROE?
options: Because they measure different things: one the price, one the efficiency of capital
Because the two ratios use different units and so cannot be added or subtracted
Because P/E is only for listed companies while ROE is for unlisted ones
Because ROE is published quarterly while P/E is only calculated at year end
quiz.explanation: ROE answers 'does this company use capital efficiently', P/E answers 'what is the market charging for that efficiency'. A company with a high ROE is still a poor investment if you overpay for it.

keyTakeaways: P/E: what you pay for each unit of profit - lower is relatively cheaper, but compare within the sector
ROE: how efficiently shareholders' money generates profit - higher is better within the same sector
D/E: how much debt is used - judge it by industry, since there is no universal threshold

practicePrompt.question: You are comparing two manufacturers in the same sector: company M has P/E 10, ROE 22%, D/E 0.4. Company N has P/E 25, ROE 8%, D/E 3.0. On these three ratios, which looks the more attractive investment?
options: Company M wins on all three: a lower P/E, a much higher ROE, and a D/E far below company N's
Company N is more attractive, because a higher P/E is always without exception a sign that the market values that company more highly
Both companies are equally attractive, because comparing financial ratios between companies in one sector is unnecessary
No conclusion is possible about which is more attractive without first knowing the market capitalisation of each one
practicePrompt.explanation: A lower P/E, a higher ROE and a lower D/E all point to company M on every one of the three criteria - this is how several ratios are combined for a judgement rather than reading one number alone.

summary.keyIdea: P/E: what you pay for each unit of profit - lower is relatively cheaper, but compare within the sector
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: ROE: how efficiently shareholders' money generates profit - higher is better within the same sector

application.title: Look it up now
application.message: Open the financial statements of a share you are considering, calculate ROE yourself (net profit / shareholders' equity), and compare it with a company in the same sector.
application.secondary: Only same-sector comparison is meaningful - don't compare a bank's ROE with a technology company's.

sections.text: Before buying any share, you only need to answer three basic questions: what am I paying for each unit of profit (P/E), how efficiently does the company use shareholders' money (ROE), and how much debt is it carrying (D/E)? These three numbers do not replace deep analysis, but they are enough to avoid the most basic mistakes.
ROE - the measure of capital efficiency

ROE (return on equity) = net profit / shareholders' equity. An ROE of 20% means the company generates 20 dong of profit for every 100 dong shareholders put in. Take two retailers with similar revenue: company A has an ROE of 25%, company B only 8% - A is using each unit of shareholder capital far more efficiently, even though the revenue lines look alike. Higher ROE is better, but compare within a sector, because capital intensity differs between industries.
D/E - leverage has to be read by industry

A high D/E (debt to equity) is not automatically bad. Banks run very high D/E because the business is taking deposits and lending them on - that is normal for the sector. But a manufacturer or technology company with a D/E unusually high against its peers is a signal to be careful: the risk of failing to service debt if rates rise or revenue drops.

Compare company A (P/E 12, ROE 18%, D/E 0.5) with company B (P/E 30, ROE 6%, D/E 2.5) in the same retail sector. A wins on all three: relatively cheaper (lower P/E), three times more efficient with capital (higher ROE), and several times safer (D/E five times lower). When all three point the same way, the signal is far more reliable than any single ratio on its own.

items: P/E: always compare against the sector average, never against an absolute number
ROE: favour companies with a high, stable ROE across years, and be suspicious of one exceptional year followed by a fall
D/E: check it against sector rivals before calling it high or low
Never decide on a single ratio - look at all three together
If the three contradict each other (a cheap P/E with low ROE and high D/E), dig deeper rather than ignoring it
